summary: GQ Atlas lets users select variables (such as surface temperature) and explore how they change over time. Users can visualize these changes through an interactive timeline on a world map or a time-series graph, if they wish. This allows users to view trends, track patterns, and gain a better understanding of how different variables change over time, thus achieving the objectives of the challenge.
details:
GQ Atlas is a hands-on platform that allows individuals to learn how Earth's climate is changing, where changes are occurring, and whether they are statistically significant. Users can explore environmental variables such as temperature, precipitation, sea surface temperature, wind, soil moisture, and sea ice through an interactive globe or flat map. People may select a location, variable, and time period to animate changes over time, look for historical anomalies, and view climate trends in their historical context.

The platform combines publicly available datasets from NASA and NOAA, including GISTEMP, GPCP, ERSST, OISST, and NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis. Python is used to process the data, calculate anomalies, and prepare annual and seasonal records. The website applies 30-year ordinary least squares regression and Newey–West statistical analysis to calculate trend rates, confidence intervals, and p-values. It also includes experimental projections extending recent historical trends toward 2100, clearly distinguishing these statistical extrapolations from climate-model forecasts.

This flowchart demonstrates the process which users can follow in order to make use of our project.

This image demonstrates how our project makes use of data, and the process which it takes to represent the data and make projections.

We also had to make sure that the information presented was reliable and easy to interpret. This meant accounting for missing data, differences in dataset resolution, and statistical uncertainty so users could understand both what the results show and where their limitations lie. What makes our approach unique is that we bring several types of environmental data into one place and let users investigate them in different ways. They can explore changes across the globe, compare two locations side by side, track trends over different time periods, and even view statistical projections of how past trends might continue. By combining these features, we make it easier to see how different parts of the Earth's climate system are changing and how those changes vary from place to place.

Our goal is to simplify complex Earth science data and make it accessible to students, educators, and the general public. Through engaging and easy-to-understand visuals, users can graphically investigate environmental trends and develop a better understanding of current climate patterns. In turn, this helps people recognize emerging environmental challenges, make informed decisions, and develop effective strategies to address the impacts of climate change. Ultimately, we hope to encourage data-driven exploration and help people understand what is changing, where it is changing, and how significant those changes are.

The project was developed using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the website, alongside Python and scientific data-processing libraries for the backend pipeline. Geographic visualization uses D3.js, TopoJSON, and HTML Canvas.

Here is a link to the repository: https://github.com/advayc/space-apps
